questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1. It is cut into 4 equal parts, so it has 5 tick marks in all: one at 0, three in the middle, and one at 1. Maya puts her dot on the 4th tick mark, counting the tick at 0 as the 1st. Which number is her dot on?
questions.explain: On a number line you count the equal spaces, not the tick marks: from 0 the dot is 3 spaces along and each space is 1/4, so it is 3/4. Counting the tick at 0 as a step is what makes people answer 4/4.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 2. Each whole is cut into 3 equal parts. Owen starts at 0 and moves 5 equal spaces to the right. Which fraction names the point he lands on?
questions.explain: Each space is 1/3, so 5 spaces past 0 is 5/3, the same point as 1 2/3. The usual slip is counting tick marks — the tick at 0 is not a step, and counting it gives 6/3.

questions.question: A number line runs from 2 to 3. The space between 2 and 3 is cut into 8 equal parts, so there are 9 tick marks in all, one at 2 and one at 3. Ravi puts a dot on the tick mark that is 5 equal spaces to the right of 2. Which number is the dot on?
questions.explain: Start at 2 and count the equal spaces: 5 spaces of 1/8 lands on 2 5/8. The denominator comes from the 8 equal parts, not from the 9 tick marks.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 2. Each whole is cut into 2 equal parts, so the tick marks sit at 0, 1/2, 1, 1 1/2 and 2 — 5 ticks in all. Ana's dot is on the 4th tick mark, counting the tick at 0 as the 1st. Which improper fraction names Ana's dot?
questions.explain: The 4th tick is 3 half-spaces past 0, so the dot is 3/2, the same point as 1 1/2. Using the tick number 4 on top, or the 5 ticks on the bottom, both come from counting ticks instead of spaces.

questions.question: Jasmine walks 11/4 km on a trail beside the Fraser River. On a number line marked from 0 km to 4 km with each kilometre cut into 4 equal parts, which mixed number shows where she stops?
questions.explain: 11 quarter-spaces is 2 whole kilometres (8 quarters) with 3 quarters left over, so she stops at 2 3/4 km. Keep the whole and the leftover in the right places — 2 wholes, 3 quarter-spaces past 2.

questions.question: On a number line from 0 to 3 marked in fifths, point P sits at 2 3/5. Which improper fraction names the very same point P?
questions.explain: Each whole is 5 fifths, so 2 wholes is 10/5, and 10/5 plus 3/5 is 13/5. The common trap is multiplying the whole by the numerator (2 times 3) instead of by the denominator.

questions.question: A metre-stick number line is taped along the classroom floor and marked in small equal parts. Which of these numbers lands strictly between the 2 1/2 m mark and the 3 m mark, not on either one?
questions.explain: Rewrite each as a mixed number: 11/4 = 2 3/4, which is past 2 1/2 but not yet 3. Careful with 5/2 — it is exactly 2 1/2, so it sits right on the mark instead of between the marks.

questions.question: Four students each marked one number on the same number line: 9/4, 2 1/4, 18/8 and 2 1/2. Three of them landed on exactly the same point. Which number landed somewhere else?
questions.explain: Change them all to quarters: 9/4, 2 1/4 and 18/8 are all the same point, 2 1/4, but 2 1/2 is 10/4, one quarter-space farther right. Equivalent fractions always land on the same point of a number line.

questions.question: Ben wants to mark 3/4 on a number line that runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 4 equal parts, giving 5 tick marks in all. He counts the tick marks 1, 2, 3 — starting with the tick at 0 — and puts his dot on that tick. Which statement is true?
options: His dot is at 2/4; he needed to count 3 equal spaces after 0, not 3 ticks.
His dot is correct, because 3/4 is always the 3rd tick mark.
His dot is at 1/4, because he should have counted back from the tick at 1.
His dot is at 3/5, because the number line has 5 tick marks.
questions.explain: The 3rd tick counting from 0 is only 2 spaces along, so Ben actually marked 2/4. A fraction on a number line counts equal spaces from 0, so 3/4 is the tick 3 spaces to the right of 0.

questions.question: On the trail at Burnaby Lake a sign stands every 1/2 km from the start at 0 km to the lookout at 4 km, so there are 9 signs, counting the sign at 0 km and the one at 4 km. Maya rests at the 6th sign, counting the sign at 0 km as the 1st. How far has she walked?
questions.explain: Count the gaps between signs, not the signs: from the 1st sign to the 6th there are 5 gaps of 1/2 km, so she has walked 5/2 km = 2 1/2 km. Treating 6 signs as 6 half-kilometres is the usual slip.

questions.question: Two number lines are drawn one under the other, both running from 0 to 1. The top line is cut into 4 equal parts and the bottom line into 8 equal parts. Priya says 3/4 on the top line lines up with the 3rd tick mark on the bottom line, counting the tick at 0 as the 1st. Is she right?
options: Yes — the 3rd tick mark is 3/4 on any number line, because the numerator 3 tells you which tick to stop at.
No — 3/4 lands on the 8th tick mark of the bottom line, because the denominator 8 names the tick it sits on.
No — 3/4 is the same point as 6/8, so it sits 6 equal spaces to the right of 0 on the bottom line.
No — 3/4 lands halfway between the 3rd and 4th tick marks on the bottom line, because 3/4 is between 3 and 4.
questions.explain: 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent, so they land on the same point: 6 of the 8 equal spaces past 0. Priya counted tick marks instead of spaces, which puts her dot on 2/8.

questions.question: A number line is painted on the gym floor at Leo's school, running from 0 m to 4 m with each metre cut into 3 equal parts. Leo stands on the mark at 2/3 m and hops 5 equal spaces to the right. Which number is he standing on now, as a mixed number?
questions.explain: Each space is 1/3 m, so 5 hops move him 5/3 m: 2/3 + 5/3 = 7/3 = 2 1/3 m. The mark he starts on is not a hop — counting it as one leaves him a third short at 2 m.
